children: Coal-based generation rose 13 per cent as transport constraints limited replenishment, leaving 51 plants with critically low stocks during August

Coal inventories at India’s thermal power plants fell around 42 per cent year-on-year to 29 million tonnes (MT) in August 2026 from 50 MT a year earlier, as higher electricity demand pushed up coal-based power generation and consumption, according to a Crisil Intelligence report.

Coal stock cover at power plants nearly halved to nine days from 17 days a year earlier, marking the lowest level since November 2023. The decline was concentrated among plants dependent on domestic coal, highlighting challenges in replenishing inventories as coal consumption increased during the period.

Between April and August, coal consumption by thermal power plants rose around 8 per cent year-on-year to 395 MT, while electricity demand increased 9.5 per cent. The rise in demand was driven by an unusually hot summer and a below-normal southwest monsoon, with cumulative rainfall between June and August 13 per cent below the long-period average.

Overall power generation increased around 10.5 per cent year-on-year during the five months, while renewable energy generation rose 20.7 per cent. Despite faster growth in renewable generation, coal-fired power continued to play a critical role in meeting round-the-clock electricity demand, keeping pressure on thermal plant inventories.

In August, 51 of the country’s 190 thermal power plants were operating with critically low coal stocks, compared with 20 plants a year earlier. Most of these facilities depend on domestic coal, making the availability of transportation and timely replenishment important for maintaining adequate stock levels.

The Central Electricity Authority considers coal stocks at power plants critical when they fall 25 per cent below the normative level. Inventory pressure was particularly high in Rajasthan, where around 72 per cent of coal-based generation capacity was operating with critically low stocks, followed by Madhya Pradesh at 69 per cent and Andhra Pradesh at 60 per cent.

Bihar and Jharkhand also reported substantial pressure, with 45 per cent and 48 per cent of their coal-based capacity, respectively, operating with critically low stocks. The situation was less pronounced in Odisha and West Bengal, where only 10 per cent and 6 per cent of coal-based capacity, respectively, was in the critical category.

Crisil Intelligence Director Sehul Bhatt said pithead coal inventories moderated from a peak of 157 MT in early March 2026 to around 76 MT in August. The decline reflected the normalisation of elevated stocks accumulated earlier in the year, rather than a broad deterioration in coal availability.

Bhatt said current pithead inventories remained broadly aligned with the average of 76.1 MT recorded across August 2024 and 2025. He said the inventory position indicated that coal availability remained adequate despite the drawdown and that there was no material supply-side stress.

The report identified a mismatch between rising electricity demand and transportation capacity as the key challenge affecting coal inventories at thermal power plants. Prolonged rainfall across the eastern coal belt disrupted mining operations and hampered coal evacuation, restricting the pace at which supplies could reach generating stations.

Between April and August, rake loading increased around 5 per cent, while coal receipts at power plants rose only 3 per cent. This was slower than the 8 per cent increase in coal consumption, leaving incremental evacuation insufficient to replenish inventories at power plants at the required pace.

To ease the situation, Coal India permitted power plants with fuel supply agreements to lift additional coal by road alongside rail transportation from September 7, 2026. The additional road movement is expected to supplement rail-based evacuation and support supplies to plants facing lower inventory levels.

Crisil Intelligence Associate Director Surbhi Kaushal expects electricity demand, coal-based generation, coal consumption and coal dispatches to power plants to grow in a narrow range of 6-7 per cent year-on-year during the second half of the fiscal year. Power demand is estimated at 860-870 billion units during the period.

Coal-based generation is expected to retain a 65-70 per cent share of India’s electricity mix, according to the report. Kaushal said adequate inventories at miners and improving evacuation logistics should allow higher dispatch requirements to be met comfortably, reducing the likelihood of prolonged inventory pressure.

The report views the recent decline in power plant coal stocks as a temporary logistical issue rather than a structural supply constraint. However, adverse weather could disrupt mining and evacuation further, while delays in improving rail availability and rake loading capacity could prolong pressure on plant-level inventories.

Crisil Intelligence said sustained higher coal dispatches would be essential to rebuild power plant stocks towards the historical average cover of 16-18 days. The pace of evacuation and replenishment will remain important as coal-based generation continues to meet a significant share of India’s electricity demand.
